content: The standard is designed to protect workers' health and safety over an 8-hour workday and a 40-hour workweek throughout their working lifetime. 3. The standard is measurable using valid, reproducible, and accessible techniques for both industry and government agencies. 4. Current technology is sufficient to enable compliance with the recommended standard. 5. 6. Inorganic lead refers to lead oxides, metallic lead, and lead salts (including organic salts like lead soaps but excluding lead arsenate). 7. 8. Lower environmental concentrations of lead do not require adherence to the outlined sections, except for Section 7(a). 9.15 mg Pb/m³, determined as a time-weighted average (TWA) over an 8-hour workday. 10. Procedures for collecting environmental samples must follow those provided in Appendix I or an equivalent method. 11. Analysis of samples must adhere to methods specified in Appendix II or any method proven to be equivalent in precision and accuracy. 12. Medical monitoring, including biologic monitoring and medical examinations, must be made available to workers as outlined. 13. 14. Unacceptable lead absorption, posing a risk of lead poisoning, is demonstrated at levels of 0.080 mg Pb/100 g of whole blood or greater, or 0.20 mg Pb/liter of urine (corrected to a specific gravity of 1.024) or greater. 15. Blood or urine sampling and analysis procedures must follow those described in Appendix II or equivalent methods. 16. Spot urine specimens of approximately 100 ml should be collected during a workday, and samples with a specific gravity less than 1.010 should be discarded and replaced. 17. Half of all workers exposed to inorganic lead must be offered biologic monitoring every six months, ensuring each worker undergoes blood sampling and analysis annually. 18. If urine sampling and analysis are chosen instead of blood lead sampling, workers must have urine sampling and analysis available every six months. 19. The biologic monitoring schedule may be altered based on findings from a professional industrial hygiene survey. 20. If environmental sampling shows levels at or above the environmental limit, biologic monitoring intervals must be halved, with blood analysis conducted quarterly and each worker sampled semi-annually. 21. Increased monitoring frequency must continue for at least six months after high environmental levels are confirmed. 22. If a worker's urine lead level is 0.20 mg/liter or greater (corrected to a specific gravity of 1.024), a blood sample must be obtained and analyzed within two weeks. 23. If a blood lead level of 0.080 mg Pb/100 g or greater is found and confirmed by a second sample within two weeks, steps to reduce lead absorption must be taken immediately. 24. 25. Workers with confirmed high biologic lead levels must undergo medical examinations for possible lead poisoning, and the OSHA area industrial hygienist must be informed of the results. 26. 27. Medical examinations must be available when administrative controls or respiratory protection are used, for workers with unacceptable lead absorption, or when environmental levels meet or exceed the standard. 28. Medical examinations should be conducted before employee placement and annually thereafter, including physical exams, complete blood counts, blood lead determinations, routine urinalysis, and documentation of any signs or symptoms of lead poisoning. 29. Workers absorbing unacceptable lead levels must be examined promptly and at least every three months until their blood or urine lead levels return to normal. 30. Workers developing clinical evidence of lead poisoning must remain under a physician's care until recovery or maximal improvement occurs, in accordance with applicable Workman’s Compensation provisions. 31. Medical records must include all biologic determinations and required medical examinations, and these records must be accessible to medical representatives of the employer, the Secretary of Labor, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, and the employee's physician upon request. 32. 33. 34. Engineering controls must be used wherever feasible to maintain lead dust and fume concentrations below prescribed limits. 35. 36. 37. 38. Local exhaust ventilation systems must be designed and maintained to prevent lead dust and fume accumulation, and air from these systems must not be recirculated into the workroom or discharged outside in a way that creates air pollution. 39. 40. Employers must monitor environmental lead levels at least every six months, with increased frequency if levels meet or exceed the standard. 41.
